title: The Goddess in All Beings
hookLine: the gods bow to the goddess in all beings, even as hunger, sleep and error, and she answers Shumbha with a vow
carry: ya devi sarvabhuteshu: the goddess in every being
tomorrow: Shumbha sends an army to drag her in by the hair. what face does she show?

cards: To the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness: bow to her, bow to her, bow to her, again and again. That's the shape of a refrain the gods sing in the fifth chapter, changing one word each time.
The third story has begun. Two demon brothers, Shumbha and Nishumbha, have taken heaven, seized the work of the sun, the moon and the wind, and thrown the gods out. So the gods do what they promised.
They remember her, go to the Himalaya, and start to sing.

teach.b: Listen to what changes. In paraphrase: the goddess who lives in all beings as consciousness. As understanding.
And, near the end, as error. Each time: bow to her, again and again. It isn't only the noble things.

teach.h: AS HUNGER, AS SLEEP, AS ERROR.
teach.b: Hunger is there, and sleep, and thirst. Even error. In this hymn the goddess isn't up on a mountain away from ordinary life; she's in the states a living being passes through in a day.
It's one of Hinduism's biggest ideas, in the goddess's language: the divine isn't somewhere else. She is in every being, in every state, even the ones we're embarrassed by. Then the story moves.
Parvati, Shiva's wife, comes down to bathe in the Ganges and asks: who are you praising?

teach.h: A GODDESS STEPS OUT OF PARVATI.
teach.b: From her own body a goddess steps out and answers: this hymn is for me. Shumbha's servants, Chanda and Munda, see her and tell their master: a king who owns every treasure should have her too.
So Shumbha sends a messenger with a proposal: marry me, or my brother. The goddess smiles. In paraphrase: what you say is true.
But long ago, without much thought, I made a vow.
Only the one who defeats me in battle, who takes away my pride, who is my equal in strength, can be my husband.

teach.h: BOW TO HER, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Let him come and win me. The messenger warns her she's being foolish. She doesn't move.

how: The refrain of the fifth chapter, beginning 'ya devi sarvabhuteshu', is also chanted on its own by some Hindus, at home and in temples, including during Navaratri.

o: a hymn-filled text on the glory of the goddess
a refrain sung only by Shiva's wife Parvati
a demon king's proposal to marry the goddess

games.q: the third story begins — tap the pairs.
p: only one who defeats me in battle

s: the hymn names only noble qualities like peace and faith
it also names hunger, sleep, thirst, shadow, and even error.
a goddess steps out of Parvati's body to answer who the hymn is for
she says this hymn is for her.
she answers with a vow: only one who defeats her in battle can be her husband.

games.q: Nani is chanting ya devi sarvabhuteshu and your cousin asks: why bow to the goddess as hunger and sleep? aren't those just... normal? what do you say?
o: that's the point: she lives in every being and every state, not only the holy ones.
they're tests the goddess sends to make us weak.
he misheard. the refrain only names noble things.
games.why: the refrain bows to her in all beings as consciousness, sleep, hunger, thirst, patience, peace, even error: no state of a living being is outside her.

practice: Notice what's here, one state at a time, the way the hymn lists them: hunger, tiredness, some patience, some restlessness, a memory, each given a breath. Don't sort them into good and bad; the hymn didn't.
If you pray, bow inwardly to the goddess at each one, as the gods do; if not, simply let each be seen.

wordCard.voice: The Devi Mahatmya. Today, ya devi sarvabhuteshu: the goddess who lives in all beings, even as hunger and error, and her vow to Shumbha.

orig.note: Sanskrit: yā devī sarvabhūteṣu, 'the goddess who in all beings…', the opening of each line of the refrain.

carryVoice: Your line: ya devi sarvabhuteshu, the goddess in every being. Hunger, sleep, even error: the hymn bows to her in them all. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Devi Mahatmya, chapter 5 (the gods' refrain; Parvati and Ambika; Shumbha's messenger)
